passage: Every evening at 8:30, Noor sat at the small table by the window of her Pune flat, set a timer on her phone for fifteen minutes and opened a green notebook. Tonight the list ran fast: the rent going up, her father's knee, a vague line her manager Thomas had written in the review, the scooter's odd rattle. When the timer was half done she drew a tick beside the two she could do something about. She wrote one small step next to the review line: "Ask Thomas for a ten-minute call on Friday." Beside her father's knee she wrote, "Not mine to fix tonight. Tomorrow's slot." At the beep she closed the notebook. At 10:40, lying awake, the knee came back to her. She whispered, "8:30 tomorrow," and turned over.

qa.q: What did Noor write next to the review line?
qa.a: She wrote, "Ask Thomas for a ten-minute call on Friday."

qa.q: Why does closing the notebook at the beep make sense to Noor, even though her worries are not solved?
qa.a: She has already turned the useful worries into a next step, so going over them again would only be spinning. Saying "8:30 tomorrow" lets her trust that the rest has a place to go.

qa.q: At 10:40 the knee worry came back. What choice did Noor make then, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She chose to send it back to tomorrow's slot instead of starting to think it through in bed. That kept the worry from taking over her night.

qa.q: How might Thomas experience the Friday call Noor is planning?
qa.a: Thomas gets a clear, short question about the review line instead of a tense or silent team member, and may be glad of the chance to explain what the line meant.

grounding: It shows an adult keeping a timed worry slot, ticking the worries she can act on, taking one step and sending the rest back to the slot.

passage: I'm Samir, and last winter I was the man who worried in the shower, on the bus and at 3 a.m. My flatmate Francis suggested something that sounded too neat to work. He said, "Give worry an appointment." So I did. Seven p.m., the kitchen, a cheap notebook, fifteen minutes on the microwave timer. I wrote everything: my visa papers, my sister's exam, a cough that wouldn't go. Then I split the page. Left side, things I could move. Right side, things I couldn't. The visa form went left, and I filled it in that night. My sister's exam went right. Some days the right side was longer, and that stung. But when a worry showed up at work, I'd tell myself, "Seven o'clock," and most days it actually waited. Francis still teases me about the microwave.

qa.q: Where and when did Samir keep his worry appointment?
qa.a: Seven p.m., in the kitchen, with a cheap notebook and fifteen minutes on the microwave timer.

qa.q: Why did it sting Samir when the right side of the page was longer?
qa.a: It meant many of his worries were things he could not change, which is hard to accept. He still kept those worries on the page rather than turning them over all day.

qa.q: Which step turned the list from a page of fears into something useful for Samir?
qa.a: Splitting the page into things he could move and things he couldn't, then acting on one, like filling in the visa form that night.

qa.q: How might Francis have seen Samir before and after the appointment idea?
qa.a: Before, Francis lived with a flatmate who was worried and distracted at all hours. After, he sees Samir calmer and can joke about the microwave, which shows the change was real.

grounding: A young adult keeps a timed evening worry slot, sorts worries into those he can and cannot act on, acts on one and lets the others wait.

passage:
Staff counsellor's notes, Rashmi, bank training centre, Mysuru
Jeevan, a probationary officer, came in for his third session today. Two weeks ago he described worrying "all day, in every meeting." Last week we set up a fifteen-minute worry slot at 6 p.m., on the bench by the parking lot, notebook in hand.
Today he showed me the pages. Each evening he writes every worry, then puts an S beside the ones he can solve. On Monday, "branch posting unclear" got an S; he emailed the personnel section next morning and had an answer by lunch. "Mother's knee" got no S; he wrote, "Call her Sunday. Rest goes to the slot." He said that when a worry pops up at 11 a.m., he tells it, "Six o'clock," and mostly it waits.
He still has hard days. At the next session we'll look at what happens on those.

qa.q: What letter does Jeevan put beside the worries he can solve?
qa.a: He puts an S beside the ones he can solve.

qa.q: How can you tell Jeevan feels more in control than he did two weeks ago?
qa.a: He now tells a mid-morning worry "Six o'clock" and it mostly waits, instead of worrying all day in every meeting.

qa.q: Why does splitting worries into S and no-S help Jeevan?
qa.a: It sends solvable ones like the branch posting straight to action and parks the rest in the slot, so real planning happens without endless spinning.

qa.q: How might Jeevan's colleagues notice the change in meetings?
qa.a: They would likely find him more present and focused, since his worries no longer pull at his attention all day.

grounding: A counsellor records an adult using a fifteen-minute worry slot, marking solvable worries, acting on one and leaving the rest for the slot.

passage:
Wednesday, 9:20 p.m.
Did my worry window tonight, 9 to 9:15, kitchen timer. Pradeep laughed when he saw me set it, but whatever.
The list:
1. Thesis draft due in three weeks.
2. Landlord might raise the rent.
3. Didn't return Nani's call.
4. That weird noise in the bike.
5. What if I never get a proper job.
Then the marking. Can I do something about it this week? 1: yes. 3: yes. 4: yes. 2 and 5: not really.
So I called Nani right then (twenty minutes on her tomato plants 😊) and booked the bike shop for Saturday. The thesis one became a step: write the methods section tomorrow before lunch.
2 and 5 stay on the page. If they turn up at 2 a.m., they can wait for tomorrow's window.
Weirdly lighter. Pradeep asked if I'd help with his list next week.
Siddharth

qa.q: What did Siddharth book for Saturday?
qa.a: Siddharth booked the bike shop for Saturday.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth feel "weirdly lighter" after the window?
qa.a: Three worries had turned into actions and the other two had a place to wait, so Siddharth's mind no longer had to carry everything at once 😊

qa.q: What could Siddharth do if worries 2 and 5 turn up at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: Siddharth could note them for tomorrow's window and gently go back to sleep, since those are not problems that can be solved at night.

qa.q: Why might Pradeep have gone from laughing to asking for help with a list?

grounding: An adult writes worries in a timed window, marks which can be acted on, acts on some and leaves the rest for the next window.

passage: Every evening at seven, after the school bell had stopped ringing in his head, Akash sat on the steps of his rented room in Almora with a small notebook and a steel cup of tea. His landlady, Rukmini aunty, watched from her kitchen window the first few days, curious. Akash wrote for exactly fifteen minutes. The inspection next month. His mother's knees. Whether the Class 8 students liked him. The leaking tap. Then he took a red pen and put a star next to anything he could do something about. The tap got a star. So did the inspection. He chose one, the tap, and knocked on Rukmini aunty's door. "Can I call the plumber tomorrow?" "Of course, beta." The rest he left in the notebook. When they came back at night, he told himself, "Seven o'clock tomorrow." By the second week he was sleeping through.

qa.a: A red pen, with a star.

qa.q: How did Akash seem to feel after a couple of weeks of the routine?
qa.a: He seemed calmer and more settled, sleeping through instead of spinning at night.

qa.q: What could Akash do with the inspection worry, now that it has a star?
qa.a: He could pick one small step, like listing what the inspector checks, and do it in the next day's action slot.

passage: In the break room of the engineering firm in Toronto, Abebe set a timer on his phone: fifteen minutes. His colleague Jin raised an eyebrow. "Meditation?" "Worry time." At 1:15 every day, the bank's staff room clears out and Rukmini stays behind with a sandwich and a yellow sticky pad. Trisha, new to the branch, watched her for a week before asking.

"What's the timer for?"

"Worry window," Rukmini said. "Fifteen minutes. I write everything that's bugging me." She turned the pad around. New regional manager visiting. Leak above my bedroom window. Did I lock the cash drawer properly yesterday. Sister's college results.

Next to two items she had drawn a small tick. "These I can do something about. The leak, I'll call the building office today. The drawer, I'll check the log at two." The others had a little cloud. "These go back in the window tomorrow. Outside it, I don't chew on them."

"Does that work?"

"Mostly. Before, I spent the whole afternoon half here." The timer beeped. Rukmini folded the note into her diary and picked up the phone.

qa.q: What time does the staff room clear out every day?
qa.a: At 1:15 every day the staff room clears out.

qa.q: Why does the worry window make Rukmini feel steadier at work?
qa.a: Rukmini used to feel distracted and anxious, half present all afternoon; knowing worries have a set place lets her feel calmer and more in control.

qa.q: What could Trisha borrow from Rukmini's method?
qa.a: Trisha could write worries for a set time, tick the solvable ones, do one today and leave the clouded ones for the next window.

qa.q: How might Trisha see Rukmini's lunch habit before and after asking?
qa.a: At first Trisha probably found it curious, maybe odd; after the explanation Trisha may see it as a practical skill worth trying.

grounding: An adult writes worries in a fifteen-minute window, marks the solvable ones, acts on one and leaves the rest for the next window.

passage:
Hi Sangeeta,

You asked how I'm handling the move to Hyderabad without losing my mind. Honestly, I was losing it. Every night at 2 a.m. my brain ran the list: the new team, the flat, whether Papa will manage the stairs at home without me, whether I'll make any friends.

So I tried something my cousin swore by. Every evening at seven I sit with tea and a notebook for exactly fifteen minutes. I write every worry. Then I put an S next to the ones I can solve. Yesterday the S ones were "book the packers" and "ask the landlord about a gas connection". I did the first one right away.

The rest, like friends and Papa, I leave in the notebook. If they come at 2 a.m., I tell myself: seven o'clock tomorrow.

It isn't magic. But I slept six hours straight last night, first time in weeks.

Write soon,
Urmila

qa.a: Urmila puts an S next to the solvable ones.

passage:
Tarun, you asked how I got through planning my brother's wedding while working full time. I'll tell you, because for about a month I did not get through it well.

I'm Urmila, by the way, the sister who ended up doing everything. The caterer, the relatives from Nagpur, the rain forecast, what if the hall double-booked. I worried in the shower, in meetings, in the auto.

Then my manager, of all people, said, "Give your worries an appointment." So I did. Every morning, 8:30 to 8:45, on the office terrace. I'd write everything. I'd circle what I could act on that day, maybe calling the hall to confirm in writing. I'd do that one thing before ten.

Rain forecast? Not solvable. Relatives' moods? Not solvable. Those stayed on the page until tomorrow's 8:30.

I won't pretend I was calm at the wedding. But I was there. I danced.

qa.q: Where did Urmila write the worries every morning?
qa.a: Every morning, 8:30 to 8:45, on the office terrace.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling before giving worries an appointment?
qa.a: Urmila felt overwhelmed and anxious, worrying in the shower, in meetings and in the auto about the caterer, relatives and rain.

qa.q: Which choice made the biggest difference in Urmila's approach, and why?
qa.a: Circling what could be acted on and doing that one thing before ten mattered most, because it turned worry into progress while unsolvable items waited.

qa.q: What would change for Tarun if Tarun tried the same appointment idea?
qa.a: Tarun might find worries easier to separate into doable steps and things to set aside, though it may take practice before it feels natural.

grounding: An adult tells how a fixed fifteen-minute worry time, acting on one solvable item and leaving the rest, helped during wedding planning.

I'm Sahil, and I've shared a flat with Abhinav for a year. He used to worry out loud all day. The rent. His mother's knee. His appraisal. Whether the landlord would sell the flat.
Since March he's been doing something new. Every evening at seven he sits at the dining table with a blue notebook and a timer set for fifteen minutes. He writes, fast. Then he goes down the list with a pencil and puts a small S next to some lines. I asked once. "Solvable," he said.
Then he picks one S and does it right there. Last week it was emailing his manager for an appraisal date. Another day, booking his mother's check-up.
When the timer beeps, he closes the notebook. If he starts worrying at dinner, he says, "That's for seven o'clock."
I can't tell what's in his head. But he laughs more at dinner now.

He wrote everything: the deposit might not come back, the new flat was farther from work, the fridge might get scratched, Mohit's cousin might not return the van on time, his manager might mind if he left early Friday.
